note_claims.claim: The patient is presenting for a diabetes review following a hypoglycaemic episode.
The hypoglycaemic episode occurred last Tuesday after skipping lunch while gardening, resulting in symptoms of being sweaty, shaky, and unable to think straight.
The patient's daughter (who has type 1 diabetes) found him confused, measured a capillary glucose of 2.8 mmol/L, and treated him with orange juice and biscuits.
The patient recovered from the hypoglycaemia within 15 minutes.
The patient experiences occasional pre-meal wobbliness.
The patient has no neuropathic symptoms.
The patient has no visual problems, and retinal screening is due.
The patient is prescribed Metformin 1g twice daily.
The patient is prescribed Gliclazide 80 mg twice daily.
The patient is prescribed Atorvastatin 20 mg.
The patient is prescribed Ramipril 5 mg.
The patient has no known drug allergies.
Pedal pulses are palpable.
Monofilament sensation is normal in both feet.
There is a callus under the ball of the left first metatarsal head.
Blood pressure is 138/84.
The patient's weight is 91 kg.
HbA1c is 62 mmol/mol, which is an increase from the previous level of 58.
The eGFR is 52, which is stable.
The patient has Type 2 diabetes with recent hypoglycaemia on gliclazide.
The HbA1c is above the target.
The patient has stable CKD stage 3a.
The patient has a low-risk foot with a callus.
The plan is to reduce gliclazide to 80 mg in the morning only.
The plan is to start empagliflozin 10 mg once daily.
Sick day rules have been explained and a leaflet has been given.
A referral to a podiatrist has been made for the callus.
The patient is scheduled for a review in three months with repeat HbA1c and kidney function tests.
The patient must check blood glucose before driving and every two hours on long journeys.
The patient must not drive if blood glucose is below 5 mmol/L.
The patient must keep fast-acting glucose in the car.
The patient should stop empagliflozin if they are unwell, not eating, or unable to drink.

transcript_facts.fact: The clinician greeted Mr Elsworth-Mahmood.
The patient's daughter, Yasmin, came because of an incident last week.
The patient experienced symptoms including being sweaty, shaky, and unable to think straight.
The hypoglycaemic episode occurred on Tuesday because it was bin day and the patient had skipped lunch.
The patient had been in the garden all morning and skipped lunch.
The relative found the patient confused and identified it as a hypoglycaemia, stating they have type 1 diabetes.
The relative gave the patient orange juice and biscuits.
The patient recovered within about fifteen minutes.
The relative measured the capillary glucose at 2.8.
The patient reported feeling 'a bit wobbly' before tea sometimes.
The patient drives to the shops and to their allotment.
The patient confirmed they were not driving that day.
The clinician checked the patient's medication and confirmed they are on Metformin 1 gram twice a day.
The clinician checked the patient's medication and confirmed they are on Gliclazide 80 milligrams twice a day.
The patient confirmed the Gliclazide timing is morning and teatime.
The clinician checked the patient's medication and confirmed they are on Atorvastatin 20 milligrams and Ramipril 5 milligrams.
The patient confirmed taking all those medications.
The patient reported no known drug allergies.
The patient reported that their feet have been fine.
The relative reported having pins and needles in their hands at night, which they suspect is carpal tunnel.
The patient confirmed they have no visual problems, but their eye screening is due.
The clinician noted the patient's HbA1c is 62, which is up from 58 last time.
The clinician noted the patient's eGFR is 52, which is about the same as before.
The clinician noted that sugar control has drifted up a little, but the hypoglycaemia worries them more.
The clinician examined the patient's feet and noted a bit of hard skin, a callus, under the ball of the left foot, by the big toe.
The clinician noted the patient's blood pressure is 138 over 84 and their weight is 91 kilos.
The clinician suggested reducing Gliclazide to 80 milligrams in the morning only and stopping the teatime dose.
The clinician suggested adding empagliflozin 10 milligrams once a day to help sugars and protect heart and kidneys.
The clinician advised stopping empagliflozin if the patient is unwell, not eating, or unable to drink.
The clinician instructed the patient to check blood sugar before driving and every two hours on long journeys.
The clinician instructed the patient not to drive if blood sugar is below five.
The clinician instructed the patient to always keep some sugary snacks in the car.
The clinician will refer the patient to a podiatrist for the callus.
The clinician instructed the patient to book their eye screening.
The clinician scheduled a follow-up in three months with a repeat HbA1c and kidney test.

findings.transcript_evidence: Relative: I'm the one with pins and needles. I get it in my hands at night. Carpal tunnel, they reckon.
findings.rationale: A relevant symptom (pins and needles/carpal tunnel) reported by the relative was omitted from the history section.
